question: Which layers are likely to become commodities?
answer: Fixed-capability model inference (prices falling ~10x/yr), mid-tier models (open weights months behind), and agent frameworks/orchestration code. Commoditization follows the capability frontier down: last year's frontier is this year's commodity.
basis: Price series and open-closed gap data 2023–26; the models-commoditize thesis is validated on price.

question: Which layers have durable technical barriers?
answer: Leading-edge semiconductors and packaging, power-ready data-center capacity, and frontier training (capital + talent + RL environments). These are physical or capital barriers, not algorithmic ones — algorithms diffuse in months.
basis: Infra-supercycle and power-binding theses validated; DeepSeek shows algorithmic leads are short-lived.

question: Where are the next architectural discontinuities likely?
answer: Memory and continual learning, RL from experience, and world models for physical tasks — the ingredients that LLM skeptics and DeepMind researchers have named for a decade. Expect them as additions to transformer systems before replacements.
basis: Historically, skeptics correctly identified missing pieces (reasoning, search) that were then added to LLMs, not substituted.

question: Where is value created vs captured?
answer: Value is created in applications and end-user productivity but, through 2026, captured mainly by chips (Nvidia), clouds and two-to-three frontier labs. Capture has migrated up the stack slowly and in sequence.
basis: Nvidia data-center revenue vs lab run-rates vs app-layer revenue, 2023–26.

question: Where could overinvestment compress margins?
answer: GPU leasing and neocloud capacity financed with debt, and any capacity built ahead of power and demand. Short GPU economic lives make overbuild costly; the 2027–29 window decides it.
basis: Capex-payback thesis unresolved; credit stress signals in late 2025.

question: Which parts of the stack have attractive long-term economics?
answer: Scarce physical inputs (advanced chips, power), distribution owners, and agent platforms that own outcomes and memory. Commodity inference and thin applications look least attractive.
basis: Consistent with which theses validated (infra, power, consolidation) vs which are contested (app moats).

question: Will hyperscalers become more powerful or less differentiated?
answer: More powerful through 2026: they control capital, power and distribution, and absorbed independent labs. Their risk is that frontier labs become platforms themselves and multi-source compute.
basis: Frontier-consolidates validated; license-and-hire deals; OpenAI's multi-cloud deals in 2025.

question: Will model providers retain durable pricing power?
answer: At the frontier tier, yes so far (rapid revenue growth despite collapsing unit prices); below it, no. Pricing power is temporary and must be re-earned each model generation.

question: How do foundation models, agents and enterprise platforms relate?
answer: Models become components; the agent layer (memory, tools, permissions) is where platform control is contested between labs, hyperscalers and SaaS incumbents.
basis: LLM-OS framing plus 2025–26 lab moves into agents and IDEs.

question: What will enterprises pay for once capability is widely available?
answer: Outcomes and reliability: completed tasks, auditability, security, integration with systems of record, and liability — not raw model access.
basis: Coding agents (outcome-shaped) are the clearest 2025–26 revenue success; generic pilots underperformed.

question: Which capabilities create measurable ROI?
answer: Software engineering first; then customer operations and document-heavy back-office work where outputs are verifiable. Open-ended knowledge work ROI remains hard to measure.
basis: Coding-first thesis validated; MIT NANDA pilot-failure findings for generic use.

question: What shifts buying from models to platforms, workflows, agents or outcomes?
answer: Model interchangeability (open weights, routing) plus agents that act on systems of record: once any model is 'good enough', buyers optimize for integration, governance and price per outcome.
basis: Commoditization of fixed capability; rise of multi-model routing.

question: Which economic assumptions are most vulnerable?
answer: That AI revenue will close a ~$600B+ annual gap fast enough to service capex and debt; that GPUs keep multi-year economic lives; and that frontier pricing power survives open competition.
basis: Capex-payback thesis unresolved; depreciation and credit concerns 2025–26.

question: Which historical investment theses have held up?
answer: Picks-and-shovels (Nvidia, 2023–26); backing frontier labs early (Microsoft/Khosla in OpenAI 2019); the power/data-center build-out (Cahn's 'shovel ready'). Independent consumer-AI and sub-scale frontier labs (Inflection, 01.AI) did not.
basis: Outcomes of strategic actions in the courtroom.

question: What leading indicators should investors track?
answer: Lab revenue run-rates vs capex guidance; open-weight lag (months); fixed-capability price decline; METR task horizons; power interconnect queues; GPU rental prices and utilization; credit spreads of AI infrastructure borrowers.
basis: These indicators would have flagged each major 2022–26 turn.
